question: Mammography of a 48-year-old woman with a palpable right breast lump shows a 15 mm irregular mass with spiculate margins and pleomorphic microcalcifications. The radiologist reports BI-RADS 5. What does this classification mandate?

answers.text: Short-interval follow-up mammography in 6 months to assess for interval change

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Short-interval follow-up is appropriate for BI-RADS 3 (probably benign). BI-RADS 5 carries ≥95% likelihood of malignancy and requires immediate tissue diagnosis, not watchful waiting.

answers.text: Tissue biopsy (core needle biopsy or vacuum-assisted biopsy) with pre-surgical staging

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. BI-RADS 5 (highly suspicious, ≥95% probability of malignancy) mandates tissue diagnosis. Core needle biopsy confirms histology, guides receptor testing, and feeds directly into staging workup (axillary ultrasound, staging CT/bone scan if indicated).

answers.text: Repeat mammography with breast MRI to better characterise the lesion before any decision

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI may be added for preoperative extent evaluation, but it should not delay tissue diagnosis. A BI-RADS 5 lesion requires biopsy, not further imaging characterisation.

answers.text: Discharge with reassurance — spiculate margins with calcifications may represent fat necrosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Spiculate margins with pleomorphic microcalcifications are highly suspicious features. BI-RADS 5 (≥95% malignancy probability) never warrants reassurance and discharge.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall the BI-RADS action mapping: 1–2 = routine screening; 3 = 6-month follow-up; 4 = biopsy; 5 = biopsy with pre-surgical staging; 6 = known biopsy-proven malignancy.
Correct. BI-RADS 5 means highly suspicious — tissue biopsy is mandatory, and the result feeds directly into staging and surgical planning.
